questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend a bar chart rather than a line plot for qubit measurement outcomes?
options: Measurement outcomes are discrete, unordered categories (e.g. 0 or 1) with no meaningful value between them, so connecting them with a line would falsely imply a continuous relationship
Matplotlib does not support line plots for numeric data below 1.0
Bar charts are required by convention and have no functional justification
Line plots can only display a single data series, while bar charts can display two
questions.explain: Outcomes like 0 and 1 (or |00>, |01>, |10>, |11>) are discrete categories, not points along a continuum, so a bar chart's separated bars correctly represent that there's nothing 'between' them.

questions.q: Given amplitude alpha = sqrt(0.3), what is P(0) = |alpha|**2, and what must P(1) equal if the state is properly normalized?
options: P(0) = 0.3, and P(1) must equal 0.7 so the two probabilities sum to 1
P(0) = 0.3, and P(1) can be any value independent of P(0)
P(0) = sqrt(0.3), since squaring is not part of the Born rule
P(0) = 0.3, and P(1) must also equal 0.3
questions.explain: Squaring sqrt(0.3) gives exactly 0.3, and for a single qubit's two possible outcomes, normalization requires P(0) + P(1) = 1, so P(1) must be 0.7.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend explicitly setting `ax.set_ylim(0, 1)` on a probability bar chart instead of letting Matplotlib auto-scale the y-axis?
options: Without a fixed 0-to-1 range, auto-scaling to the data can stretch the axis in a way that makes a large probability look small, or makes small differences between runs look exaggerated
`ax.set_ylim` is required syntax and the plot will raise an error without it
Auto-scaling always defaults to a 0-to-100 range, which is wrong for probabilities
Setting the y-limit changes the underlying probability values to sum to 1
questions.explain: Matplotlib's default auto-scaling fits the axis tightly to whatever data is plotted, which can visually mislead a reader comparing probabilities across different plots or runs unless the 0-to-1 scale is fixed explicitly.

questions.q: For a 2-qubit system with amplitudes `np.sqrt([0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4])`, what are the corresponding measurement probabilities, and do they represent a valid normalized state?
options: The probabilities are [0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4], and yes, they sum to 1.0, so the state is validly normalized
The probabilities are [0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4], but they sum to less than 1, so the state is invalid
The probabilities are the square roots of those values, since squaring was already applied when building the amplitudes
There is no way to know without running the actual quantum circuit on hardware
questions.explain: Squaring each square-rooted value simply recovers the original numbers [0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4], and 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.3 + 0.4 = 1.0, confirming a valid normalized distribution across the four 2-qubit basis states.

questions.q: In the bar-annotation example, why does the text placement use `bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2` for the x-coordinate instead of just `bar.get_x()`?
options: `bar.get_x()` alone returns the bar's left edge, so adding half its width centers the label horizontally over the middle of the bar instead of at its left edge
`bar.get_x()` returns the bar's height, not its horizontal position, so the width must be added to convert units
This calculation is unnecessary and has no effect on where the text appears
`bar.get_width()` must always be divided by 2 to convert from pixels to data coordinates
questions.explain: `bar.get_x()` gives the x-position of the bar's left edge; adding half the bar's width shifts that position to the bar's horizontal center, which is where a value label reads most naturally.
